misconceptions.statement: Every axiom must be proved from other statements before it can be used.
misconceptions.why: Students are used to every maths result being proved or derived in class.
misconceptions.fix: Axioms are basic statements accepted as true without proof; all proofs start from them.

probe.question: Can Euclid's axiom 'things equal to the same thing are equal to one another' be used without proving it first?
probe.wrong_answer: No, it must be proved first.

misconceptions.root_belief: everything accepted in a subject has been proved

misconceptions.statement: Measuring angles in a few drawn triangles with a protractor proves a theorem.
misconceptions.why: Earlier classes verified properties by measuring or paper folding.
misconceptions.fix: A theorem is proved by logical steps from axioms and earlier theorems; measuring a few cases only checks them and cannot prove it for all cases.

probe.question: You measure the angle sum in five triangles and get 180 each time. Has the angle sum property been proved?

misconceptions.root_belief: seeing examples work proves a rule always works
misconceptions.source_hint: education research on students' proof schemes (empirical vs deductive proof)

misconceptions.statement: The rule 'equals added to equals are equal' works only for numbers, not for lengths or angles.
misconceptions.why: Students link the word 'equal' only with numerical equations.
misconceptions.fix: The axiom applies to any quantities that can be compared, including lengths, angles and areas.

probe.question: AB = CD. Is AB + BC equal to CD + BC?
probe.wrong_answer: Cannot say, because these are lengths and not numbers.

misconceptions.root_belief: a rule from numbers does not apply to other quantities

misconceptions.statement: A straight line has two end points, just like a line segment.
misconceptions.why: Everyday and early-class drawings of a line are always finite with ends.
misconceptions.fix: A line extends endlessly in both directions; only a line segment has two end points.

probe.question: A line has two end points. True or false?

misconceptions.root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning
misconceptions.source_hint: studies of students' concept images of line, ray and segment

misconceptions.statement: Many different straight lines can be drawn through two given points.
misconceptions.why: Through one point many lines pass, and students carry this over to two points.
misconceptions.fix: Through two distinct points exactly one straight line can be drawn.

probe.question: How many straight lines pass through both points A and B?

misconceptions.root_belief: what holds for one case holds for the next

misconceptions.statement: Two lines meet on the side where the interior angles add up to more than 180 degrees.
misconceptions.why: Students remember '180' from the postulate but not which side the lines meet.
misconceptions.fix: The lines meet on the side where the two interior angles add up to less than 180 degrees.

probe.question: A transversal makes interior angles of 100 and 95 degrees on one side. Do the lines meet on that side?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, they meet there because the sum is more than 180.

misconceptions.root_belief: remembering a number means remembering the whole rule

misconceptions.statement: Any two adjacent angles form a linear pair.
misconceptions.why: Students remember only that a linear pair is adjacent and ignore the straight-line condition.
misconceptions.fix: A linear pair is two adjacent angles whose non-common arms form a straight line, so they add to 180 degrees.

probe.question: Angles of 50 and 60 degrees share an arm. Do they form a linear pair adding to 180?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, they are adjacent so they form a linear pair.

misconceptions.root_belief: a partial condition is the full definition

misconceptions.statement: The two angles of a linear pair are always equal, each 90 degrees.
misconceptions.why: The standard picture shows a perpendicular line on a straight line.
misconceptions.fix: The angles of a linear pair are equal only when the line is perpendicular; in general they just add to 180 degrees.

probe.question: One angle of a linear pair is 120 degrees. What is the other?

misconceptions.root_belief: the usual picture is the only case
misconceptions.source_hint: research on prototype images in geometry

misconceptions.statement: Complementary angles add up to 180 degrees.
misconceptions.why: The words complementary and supplementary sound alike and are mixed up.
misconceptions.fix: Complementary angles add to 90 degrees; supplementary angles add to 180 degrees.

probe.question: What is the complement of 70 degrees?

misconceptions.root_belief: similar-sounding terms mean the same thing
misconceptions.source_hint: common error analyses in school geometry

misconceptions.statement: Complementary or supplementary angles must be next to each other.
misconceptions.why: Textbook diagrams always show these pairs as adjacent angles.
misconceptions.fix: The angles can be anywhere; only their sum (90 or 180 degrees) matters.

probe.question: Two separate angles are 30 and 60 degrees in different figures. Are they complementary?

misconceptions.root_belief: the usual picture is the only case

misconceptions.statement: Vertically opposite angles add up to 180 degrees.
misconceptions.why: They are confused with a linear pair, since both appear where two lines cross.
misconceptions.fix: Vertically opposite angles are equal; it is the neighbouring angles (linear pair) that add to 180 degrees.

probe.question: Two lines cross and one angle is 40 degrees. What is the angle opposite to it?

misconceptions.root_belief: similar-looking cases follow the same rule
misconceptions.source_hint: misconception studies on angle relations at intersecting lines

misconceptions.statement: Vertically opposite angles are equal only when the two lines are perpendicular.
misconceptions.why: Students see equal angles mainly in the symmetric picture of crossing at 90 degrees.
misconceptions.fix: Vertically opposite angles are equal for any two intersecting lines, whatever the angle between them.

probe.question: Two lines cross at 60 degrees. Are the opposite 60-degree angles equal?
probe.wrong_answer: Not necessarily, they are equal only if the lines are perpendicular.

misconceptions.root_belief: a special case is the general rule

misconceptions.statement: Corresponding angles are equal for any two lines cut by a transversal.
misconceptions.why: Students forget the condition that the lines must be parallel.
misconceptions.fix: Corresponding angles are equal only if the two lines are parallel.

probe.question: Two non-parallel lines are cut by a transversal. Are the corresponding angles equal?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, corresponding angles are always equal.

misconceptions.root_belief: a rule works without its conditions
misconceptions.source_hint: research on students ignoring conditions in geometry theorems

misconceptions.statement: Alternate interior angles are the two angles between the lines on the same side of the transversal.
misconceptions.why: The names alternate and co-interior (same side) interior angles are mixed up.
misconceptions.fix: Alternate interior angles lie between the lines on opposite sides of the transversal.

probe.question: Lines are parallel. Two interior angles on the same side of the transversal are called alternate angles, so they are equal. Right?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, they are alternate angles and equal.

misconceptions.root_belief: angle names can be used loosely

misconceptions.statement: Co-interior angles on parallel lines are equal.
misconceptions.why: Students extend the equal-angle rule of corresponding and alternate angles to all pairs.
misconceptions.fix: Co-interior angles on parallel lines are supplementary; they add to 180 degrees.

probe.question: Parallel lines are cut by a transversal. One co-interior angle is 70 degrees. What is the other?

misconceptions.root_belief: one pattern applies to all similar cases
misconceptions.source_hint: error analyses of angle problems with parallel lines

misconceptions.statement: Parallel lines are always horizontal, so a tilted pair of lines cannot be parallel.
misconceptions.why: Textbook and board diagrams usually show parallel lines as horizontal.
misconceptions.fix: Lines in any direction are parallel if they never meet, i.e. stay the same distance apart.

probe.question: Two slanted lines both rise at the same slope. Are they parallel?
probe.wrong_answer: No, parallel lines must be horizontal.

misconceptions.root_belief: the usual picture is the only case
misconceptions.source_hint: research on prototype and orientation effects in geometry concepts

misconceptions.statement: If two lines look parallel in a figure, they are parallel and no angle check is needed.
misconceptions.why: Students trust the diagram and do not check conditions.
misconceptions.fix: Lines are shown parallel only if given or if corresponding, alternate or co-interior angles satisfy the conditions; a figure may not be to scale.

probe.question: Alternate angles are 65 and 70 degrees but the lines look parallel. Are they parallel?

misconceptions.root_belief: what looks true in a picture is true
misconceptions.source_hint: research on reliance on diagrams in geometric reasoning

misconceptions.statement: A bigger triangle has a larger angle sum than a small triangle.
misconceptions.why: Students think greater size means greater quantity.
misconceptions.fix: The angle sum of every triangle is 180 degrees, whatever its size.

probe.question: A huge triangle and a tiny triangle: which has the bigger angle sum?

misconceptions.root_belief: bigger or more means more effect
misconceptions.source_hint: studies of students confusing side length with angle size

misconceptions.statement: The angle sum of an obtuse-angled triangle is more than 180 degrees.
misconceptions.why: One large angle seems to push the total above 180.
misconceptions.fix: Every triangle, acute, right or obtuse, has angle sum 180 degrees.

probe.question: A triangle has angles 120, 30 and 30 degrees. What is its angle sum?
probe.wrong_answer: It has more than 180 because one angle is obtuse.

misconceptions.root_belief: a special case is the general rule

misconceptions.statement: An exterior angle equals the sum of its adjacent interior angle and one other interior angle.
misconceptions.why: Students mix up which interior angles are 'opposite' and which is adjacent.
misconceptions.fix: An exterior angle equals the sum of the two interior opposite angles, not including the adjacent interior angle.

probe.question: Triangle angles are 50, 60, 70. The exterior angle at the 70 angle equals?

misconceptions.root_belief: similar-sounding terms mean the same thing
misconceptions.source_hint: error analyses of triangle exterior angle problems

misconceptions.statement: An angle with longer arms is a bigger angle.
misconceptions.why: Students judge the angle by how long the drawn arms look.
misconceptions.fix: The size of an angle is the amount of turn between the arms and does not depend on how long they are drawn.

probe.question: Two angles are both 40 degrees but one has arms 10 cm long and the other 3 cm. Which is bigger?

misconceptions.root_belief: bigger or more means more effect
misconceptions.source_hint: research on children's conceptions of angle size

misconceptions.statement: Two lines that are each parallel to a third line can meet each other.
misconceptions.why: Students do not accept that parallelism passes from one line to another.
misconceptions.fix: If two lines are parallel to the same line, they are parallel to each other and never meet.

probe.question: Lines l and m are both parallel to line n. Can l and m intersect?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, they can meet if they are tilted differently.

misconceptions.root_belief: a relation does not carry over to a third thing
